extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and scientists (readers of Popular Science Monthly; members of scientific societies)
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for what counts as natural science and for good scientific practice: emphasis on induction, trained observation, avoidance of anthropomorphism, experiment, persistence, and the practical application of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Natural Science
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the term Natural Science, we here mean not only the sum of our knowledge of Nature, organic and inorganic, its phenomena, its effects, and its laws, but also the conscious insight into the one method which aids in enlarging that sum of knowledge, and also the conscious application of this knowledge to the useful arts, to navigation, medicine, etc. — in short, the mastery and exploitation of Nature by man with a view to increasing his own power, comfort, and enjoyment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this broad, two-part standard when judging whether an enterprise counts as 'science': (1) factual and theoretical knowledge of nature and its laws; (2) explicit understanding and application of the correct investigative method and practical exploitation of the resulting knowledge (e.g., in navigation, medicine, industry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction as the only safe path
rubrics_metrics.description: The painstaking assiduity required to ascend the difficult path of induction — the only safe path — from particular and sharply-circumscribed facts, up to general propositions, thus rising gradually and methodically from the apparently accidental to the conception of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer conclusions drawn by careful inductive reasoning from well-defined observations over speculative or immediate generalizations. Score higher those works that build general propositions slowly and methodically from particular, well-documented facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training of the observer (sensory/instrumental education)
rubrics_metrics.description: That the eye must be trained, we know from physiology. ... It was only two hundred years ago discovered by Mariotte, that in each eye we have a blind spot... From the year 1809, when Malus discovered the polarization of light, observers ... had vainly endeavored with the naked eye to distinguish polarized from ordinary light. But since 1844, when Haidinger succeeded in doing this, the yellow tufts which bear his name belong, for every trained eye, to the normal aspect of the blue sky.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the quality of observation by whether observers have accounted for sensory limitations and have trained or instrumented their senses appropriately. Examples/anti-patterns: failing to note blind spots, after-images, polarization, or harmonic notes; counting stars poorly due to untrained observation. Reward use of training, instruments, and techniques that reveal phenomena invisible to naive perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid anthropomorphism and personification of natural forces
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever confronted [man] in the shape of a compelling power of Nature ... he recognized the act of beings like himself ... This personificative or anthropomorphic stage ... is the origin of the idea of Force which has done so much mischief in science... What difference is there between that Will which, according to our latest Nature-philosophers, drives the atoms together, and the gods of antiquity who animated the planets?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge explanations negatively if they resort to imagining willful, human-like agents or personified forces without empirical grounding. Favor mechanistic/law-based accounts over anthropomorphic narratives; penalize appeals to 'miracle-workers' or 'will' when the phenomenon can be treated by lawlike causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conscious insight into scientific method and its application
rubrics_metrics.description: Natural science ... also the conscious insight into the one method which aids in enlarging that sum of knowledge, and also the conscious application of this knowledge to the useful arts ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether practitioners explicitly understand and apply the scientific method (experimental design, controlled observation, induction). Works that show unconscious or anecdotal practice score lower than those with explicit methodological awareness and thoughtful application to problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiment as guide to invention and inference
rubrics_metrics.description: As this is par excellence the period of unconscious inferences, so it is to be admitted that such inferences, guided by experiment, have led to the invention of the first tools. These were invented ... by many, and at points very distant from one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value experimental guidance in both theoretical inference and practical invention. Recognize that useful artifacts and techniques often arise from experimental probing; reward explicit experimental evidence linking claim to outcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persistence, assiduity, and long-term methodical effort
rubrics_metrics.description: Their minds ... lacked the painstaking assiduity required to ascend the difficult path of induction ... True, during the 1,000 years which intervened ... individual minds attained extraordinary heights. But nothing so plainly exhibits the hesitating step of natural science among the ancients as the simple fact that 400 years after Aristotle's day ... so uncritical a collector as Pliny could exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credit sustained, persistent, and systematic research efforts; penalize sporadic, non-systematic, or chance-driven collections of observations that lack methodological consistency over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic, critical observation vs. chance opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: Unfortunate, however, he observes, truth and error are here both equally the work of chance; the opinions here stated are like lottery-tickets, whose value is known only after the drawing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between carefully controlled/replicated observations and statements that amount to random conjecture. Give higher weight to results reproducible and critically examined rather than to isolated assertions whose veracity appears accidental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful measurement, counting, and attention to detail
rubrics_metrics.description: The elder Pliny states the number of observed stars ... as only 1,600; while Argelander reckoned 3,256; and Heis ... added 2,000 more. ... Hipparchus and Ptolemy take no note of the nebula in Orion, or of that in Andromeda. ... ordinary observers, with good eyesight, can discern fourteen to sixteen stars in [the Pleiades] constellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require accurate counting, careful recording of magnitudes and classes, and attention to details that naive observers miss. Use examples (star counts, nebulae) to justify emphasis on measurement accuracy and completeness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism about first/naive explanations; beware of facile hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when by chance they observed aright, their very first attempt at an explanation would involve them in a tangle of such absurd and ridiculous fancies that one much prefers the theory of old Pan ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer analyses that avoid immediate, speculative or fantastical explanations for observed phenomena. Reward hypotheses that are tested and restrained by data rather than imaginative stories or myth-like accounts; penalize reliance on the first facile explanation.
